Antarctodarwinella.note: A struthiolariid sea snail of Eocene Antarctica, a lineage that survives in New Zealand's ostrich-foot shells.

Austrochlamys.note: A cold-water scallop of the Antarctic shelf since the Miocene; its relative Adamussium colbecki grows under the sea ice today.

Bakevellia.note: A wing-shelled bivalve of lagoons and shallow shelves, in the Permian, Triassic and Jurassic of every continent.

Balaenoptera.note: The rorquals -- blue, fin, minke and humpback's kin -- lunge-feeders on krill and shoaling fish since the late Miocene.

Cassianella.note: A small pearl-oyster relative of the Cassian beds of the Dolomites, where a whole Triassic reef community is preserved shell by shell.

Cellaria.note: A jointed, bushy bryozoan of cool shelf seas; in the Southern Ocean bryozoans build the sea-floor thickets that a reef's corals build in the tropics.

Cerastoderma.note: The cockle, a shallow-burrowing clam of estuaries and brackish lagoons; the Paratethys's low salinity suited it, and its species there ran riot.

Cerithium.note: A tall-spired horn snail of warm shallow water, in vast numbers in the brackish Sarmatian sea of the Paratethys.

Cladiscites.note: A smooth, involute Late Triassic ammonoid of the Tethys and Timor, with fine spiral lines and sutures like lace.

Clione limacina.note: The sea angel, a shell-less swimming snail of the polar oceans that hunts sea butterflies with hooked tentacles.

Coelorinchus.note: A grenadier of the continental slope, its otoliths in New Zealand's Miocene mudstones by the hundred.

Coelostylina.note: A tall-spired sea snail of Triassic shelves, common enough in the Cassian and Muschelkalk faunas to be the Triassic's ordinary snail.

Crioceratites.note: An open-coiled ammonite, whorls not touching, ribbed and spined, of the Hauterivian seas of the Tethys and Neuquen.

Cyrtina.note: A small spiriferide brachiopod with a high flat beak, from the Silurian to the last Triassic sea floors.

Deshayesites.note: The ammonite that defines the base of the Aptian, in the seas that widened as the Atlantic opened south.

Diaphus.note: A lanternfish genus of a hundred living species, whose otoliths are the commonest fish fossils of Neogene deep-water sediments from New Zealand to Italy.

Dissostichus mawsoni.note: The Antarctic toothfish, a two-metre notothenioid with antifreeze in its blood, top fish predator under the Ross Sea ice.

Douvilleiceras.note: A knobbed, thick-ribbed Albian ammonite found on every continent, in the Western Interior Seaway and the Tethys alike.

Encrinus liliiformis.note: The sea lily of the Muschelkalk, whose stem ossicles make whole beds of the German Middle Triassic; the crinoid gardens of a shallow inland sea.

Eumorphotis.note: A ribbed scallop-like bivalve that crowded the sea floors of the earliest Triassic with Claraia, one of the few shells that thrived in the aftermath of the extinction.

Euphausia superba.note: Antarctic krill: swarms of hundreds of millions of tonnes on which the whole Southern Ocean food web rests.

Eurhomalea.note: A venus clam of the cold southern shelves, in Antarctic sediments from the Palaeocene onward and on Patagonian shores today.

Flexoptychites.note: A smooth, globular ceratitid ammonoid of the Middle Triassic Tethys, in the Alpine limestones by the thousand.

Gadus morhua.note: The Atlantic cod, the fish that fed and built the North Atlantic's coasts, from the Grand Banks to Lofoten.

Glyphea.note: A burrowing lobster of Jurassic and Cretaceous sea floors, whose Thalassinoides-type burrows outnumber its bodies by millions.

Gondolella.note: A conodont whose platform elements zone the Permian and Triassic worldwide; the last of the conodonts went with its family at the end of the Triassic.

Gymnotoceras.note: The Anisian ammonoid of Nevada's Fossil Hill and of Arctic Siberia, a ceratitid of the open Panthalassan and Boreal seas.

Henodus.note: A placodont with a turtle-like shell wider than long and a toothless beak, in a brackish lagoon of Late Triassic Germany.

Hypsocormus.note: A tuna-shaped pachycormid fish of the Jurassic sea, a fast predator of the same family as the giant filter-feeder Leedsichthys.

Lahillia.note: A thick-shelled clam of Seymour Island, in the Antarctic shelf sands from the last Cretaceous stage through the Eocene, before the ice.

Limacina helicina.note: The sea butterfly, a swimming snail a few millimetres across that feeds Arctic cod and whales, and whose thin shell dissolves first as the ocean acidifies.

Limopsis.note: A small, hairy-shelled clam of cool and deep water, one of the commonest bivalves of the Antarctic and subantarctic shelves.

Lobodon carcinophaga.note: The crabeater seal, the most numerous large mammal on Earth after us, sieving krill through lobed teeth on the Antarctic pack ice.

Mactra.note: Trough shells, burrowing clams of sandy shores; the Paratethys of the late Miocene was so full of them that its beds are called the Mactra limestones.

Magasella.note: A terebratulid brachiopod of New Zealand's shelves, where lamp-shells are still abundant in the cool south.

Mallotus villosus.note: The capelin, the small silver fish that cod, whales and seabirds of the North Atlantic and Arctic all depend on.

Megaptera.note: The humpback whale, with flippers a third of its length, migrating between polar feeding grounds and tropical calving waters.

Mortoniceras.note: A large keeled Albian ammonite of the Tethys, Africa and the Americas, the last zone fossil of the Early Cretaceous.

Neithea.note: A ribbed, unequal-valved scallop of Cretaceous shelves, one of the commonest bivalves of the chalk seas.

Neocomites.note: A ribbed Valanginian ammonite of the Tethys and the young Atlantic, the standard fossil of the Neocomian.

Neoschizodus.note: A trigoniid clam, ribbed and triangular, that burrowed the Triassic sands of the Tethys and the Muschelkalk sea.

Neospathodus.note: An Early Triassic conodont whose elements date the recovery from the end-Permian extinction, stage by stage, in Pakistan, China and Nevada alike.

Nothosauridae.note: Nothosaurs: long-necked, paddle-limbed reptiles of Triassic shores, seal-like in habit, from the Muschelkalk to Guizhou.

Notosaria.note: A rhynchonellid brachiopod of New Zealand and the Southern Ocean, a lamp-shell lineage still common where the water is cold.

Olcostephanus.note: A globular, strongly ribbed ammonite of the Valanginian, known from Europe to Argentina, Mexico and South Africa.

Orbitolina.note: A cone-shaped larger foraminifer of the Urgonian reefs and platforms, the rock-former of the Aptian-Albian Tethys.

Orcinus.note: The orca, the ocean's top predator, hunting from the pack ice to the tropics in family pods that pass their hunting techniques down the generations.

Oxytropidoceras.note: A sharp-keeled Albian ammonite of the Gulf Coast, Peru, Venezuela and Africa: the fauna of a tropical Atlantic that had just been made.

Pagophilus groenlandicus.note: The harp seal, whelping on the pack ice of the North Atlantic and following the ice edge through the year.

Panopea.note: The geoduck, a deep-burrowing clam with a siphon longer than its shell, in cool shelf sands from the Cretaceous to the present; the commonest fossil shell of Antarctica's Miocene.

Pleuragramma antarctica.note: The Antarctic silverfish, the herring of the Southern Ocean, the link between the krill and the penguins, seals and whales.

Polyptychites.note: A Boreal Valanginian ammonite of the northern seas, from England to Siberia and Canada, marking the province the Tethyan forms did not reach.

Psiloceras.note: The smooth ammonite whose first appearance defines the base of the Jurassic, in the first seas after the end-Triassic extinction.

Pterotrigonia.note: A winged trigoniid clam of Cretaceous shores, common in Japan and the American Gulf Coast.

Ptyktoptychion.note: A chimaera of the Eromanga sea, known from its tooth plates in the opal fields of South Australia.

Sarmatian fauna.note: The brackish Sarmatian sea of the Paratethys: no corals, no sea urchins, no ammonite kin, but cockles, trough shells and horn snails in beds a hundred metres thick.

Spondylospira.note: A Late Triassic spiriferinid brachiopod of the Panthalassan shelves, from Nevada to Peru.

Steinmanella.note: A large, heavily ribbed trigoniid clam, the shell that paves the Early Cretaceous shores of Argentina, and known too from Japan and South Africa.

Toxaster.note: A heart urchin of Early Cretaceous shelf marls, the ancestor of Micraster's line, burrowing in the Tethyan mud.

Tropaeum.note: A giant open-coiled Aptian ammonite, over a metre across in the Eromanga sea of Australia, whose shell was a slow spiral of separate whorls.

Umoonasaurus.note: A small plesiosaur of the cold Eromanga sea, found in the opal mines of Coober Pedy with crests on its skull.

Unionites.note: A small, plain clam of low-oxygen Triassic muds, tolerant enough to be almost the only shell in some Early Triassic beds.
